title: Don Quixote, pages 1–12
sub: Sixteen questions on tonight's reading, under eight minutes. The same things your reading guide asks you to look for.
cite: Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes, Core Classics abridged for young readers
note: Questions and answers are shuffled every time, so running it twice is not the same quiz twice. Get one wrong and a hint names the page.
bigq: Is Don Quixote simply imagining adventures, or does he believe they are real? Use three examples from the reading and explain your judgment.

items.q: Where does the story take place?
opts: In a village in the province of La Mancha, in Spain
In the city of Seville, on the southern coast of Spain
In a castle in the mountains above a village in Spain
On a farm in the hills of Portugal, close to the border
items.hint: The very first sentence names the province. He later puts that name into his own.
items.why: “Once upon a time there lived in a village in Spain, in the province of La Mancha.”

items.q: Who is the main character, and what is he like?
opts: A young knight called Don Belianis, about twenty, who lives alone in a great stone castle
A gentleman called Quixania, about fifty, thin but tough, and a great lover of hunting
A farmer called Amadis of Gaul, about forty, who lives with his wife and his children
A soldier called Rocinante, about sixty, who lives with his mother and his sister
items.hint: He has a lean face and is a very early riser. His household is an elderly housekeeper, a niece under twenty, and a handyman.
items.why: “His name was Quixania.” About fifty, thin but tough of body, a very early riser and a great lover of hunting.

items.q: What kind of books does he love, and what do they do to him?
opts: Histories of the kings of Spain; he sets off to join the king's army at once
Romances of chivalry; he gives up hunting and his judgment becomes warped
Books of poetry; he begins writing verses about his own neighborhood
Books about farming; he decides to grow more crops than ever before
items.hint: They are stories about knights. He even sold good cropland to buy more of them.
items.why: Romances of chivalry. He lost interest in hunting, neglected his daily concerns, and his judgment became “so warped.”

items.q: What does he decide to become?
opts: A writer of romances about knights and their adventures
A soldier in the king's army, fighting in real battles
A knight, riding about the world setting wrongs right
A farmer with far more cropland than he had before
items.hint: He wanted to do what the men in his books did, and go out seeking adventures.
items.why: He resolved “to become a knight himself and ride about the world setting wrongs right and seeking adventures.”

items.q: His armor had no helmet, so he made a visor out of cardboard. What happened when he tested it?
opts: His sword broke in half against the hard cardboard
He destroyed it with one stroke of his sword
It held up perfectly well and he was delighted
He decided it was too risky and did not test it
items.hint: He wanted to know whether it would resist cuts, so he drew his sword and struck it. It had taken him a whole week to make.
items.why: “He made a stroke at it and in one instant demolished” the work of a whole week.

items.q: What did he do about the visor after that?
opts: He gave up on cardboard and bought a real helmet in the village
He lined the cardboard with iron and did not test it again
He borrowed a proper helmet from one of his neighbors
He tested a second one and this time it held together
items.hint: He made it stronger, then made very sure he never found out whether it was strong enough.
items.why: He lined it with iron and “declared his new visor was sufficiently strong, without risking any more experiments on it.” He had already proved it useless once, and he made certain never to prove it again.

items.q: What does he name his horse, and what is the horse really like?
opts: Bucephalus; really a fine young charger that he had bought
Rocinante; really an old horse that is skin and bone
Dulcinea; really a strong horse he had raised himself
Amadis; really a horse he borrowed from a neighbor
items.hint: It had as many points as a mariner's compass, but he thought it finer than the famous horse of Alexander.
items.why: Really skin and bone. To him, a charger superior to the Bucephalus of Alexander. He sees the horse he wants, not the horse that is there.

items.q: What new name does he give himself, and why that one?
opts: Don Belianis of Spain, to honor the king that he serves
Don Quixote de la Mancha, to honor his home region
Don Amadis of Gaul, to honor the knight he admires
Don Quixote of Toboso, to honor the lady he loves
items.hint: It took him eight days. He copied the valiant Amadis, who added the name of his country to his own.
items.why: Don Quixote, enlarged to Don Quixote de la Mancha, so that he “made clear his origin and honored his country by adopting its name.”

items.q: Who is Dulcinea del Toboso really?
opts: A princess he had once met at the court of the king of Spain
A farmer's daughter called Aldonza Lorenzo
A lady who had written to him about the books he loved
His niece, who was under twenty and lived in his house
items.hint: She lived in his own neighborhood, and she did not seem to know or care anything about him.
items.why: Aldonza Lorenzo, a good-looking farmer's daughter who barely knew he existed. He gave her a name fit for a princess because a knight needed a lady.

items.q: Why does he almost turn back soon after leaving home?
opts: He remembered he had left his shield hanging up in his hall
He remembered he had never been dubbed a knight
He realised that Rocinante was too old for the journey
He saw that his visor was still only cardboard inside
items.hint: By the laws of chivalry he could wear only white armor and carry no device until he had earned one.
items.why: He had not been dubbed a knight in the proper form, so he decided to get knighted by the first knight he met.

items.q: Which road does Don Quixote take?
opts: The widest and busiest road that he could find
The road leading back toward his own village
The road that led south in the direction of Seville
Whichever road his horse chose
items.hint: He thought that letting it happen this way was the true spirit of adventure.
items.why: “He allowed his horse to follow whatever road it pleased, considering this to be the true spirit of adventure.”

items.q: He reaches an inn at nightfall. What does he think it is?
opts: A monastery where the monks would give him food and a bed for the night
A castle with four towers, silver spires, a drawbridge and a moat
A shepherd's hut of the kind he had been looking for all day
The great stone house of a giant he would have to fight
items.hint: Everything he saw was tinted and transformed by the nonsense from his books. He took the two girls at the door for damsels, and a pig-driver's horn for a trumpet announcing him.
items.why: He “at once pictured this inn as a castle with four towers, spires of polished silver, a drawbridge and moat.” An ordinary inn, seen as a castle.

items.q: Who does he ask to make him a knight, and what does that man really think of him?
opts: A passing knight, who agrees because he admires his courage
The landlord, who can see he is mad and plays along
A priest at the chapel, who refuses him at first
The lord of the castle, who believes every word he says
items.hint: He fell on his knees and begged in very flowery language. The man he asked knew the romances well and had guests to entertain.
items.why: The landlord “readily made out the kind of madness from which the stranger suffered” and played along to amuse his guests. Everybody else can see what is really going on.

items.q: Where does he put his armor for the night, and why not in the chapel?
opts: In the stable, because the chapel had been locked up for the night
In a trough in the yard, because the chapel had been demolished
On the altar, because the host led him there himself
In his room, because the host said the yard was not safe
items.hint: The host had an answer ready, and said such a thing was allowed in cases of necessity.
items.why: The chapel “had recently been demolished so that it might be rebuilt,” so he laid his armor in a trough in one of the yards.

items.q: Two mule drivers came to move his armor out of the trough. What did he do?
opts: He let them take it, since his watch was nearly finished
He knocked them out with his lance
He called the landlord to come and deal with them
He hid and watched them from the far side of the yard
items.hint: They only wanted to fetch water for their mules. The landlord had to stop the fight by telling their friends he was a madman.
items.why: He gave the first “such a thwack on the head with his lance that he was knocked out,” and the second met the same fate. He was not pretending: he hurt two real men to guard his armor.

items.q: The last page of tonight's reading is a full-page picture. What does it show?
opts: Don Quixote fighting off the angry mule drivers with his shield
Don Quixote kneeling as the innkeeper dubs him a knight
Don Quixote marching up and down in the bright moonlight
Don Quixote riding away from the inn at first light
items.hint: Look at the caption printed under the picture. He is guarding something, all night long.
items.why: The caption reads: “For hours he marched up and down in the bright moonlight.” He is watching his armor.
